items.title: Chapter 1 Overview: Getting Your First Look
items.body:
Getting Your First Look

Welcome to Windows 11. This chapter covers the absolute basics you'll use every single day: logging in, finding your way around the Desktop, using the mouse, and shutting your computer down the right way.

Learning objectives

  • Log in to the computer using a username and password
  • Describe the basic layout of the Windows Desktop screen
  • Use the mouse to right-click and drag
  • Work with the Start menu
  • Shut down the computer correctly

Logging in to Windows (Hands-On 1.1)

Logging in means entering your username and password so the computer knows it's you and connects you to the network securely. A strong password mixes uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols — never a name, birthday, or common word — and should never be shared. Password managers like 1Password, LastPass, RoboForm, or Avira can remember them for you.

  1. Turn on the computer and monitor, if necessary.
  2. Click the lock screen to bring up the sign-in screen.
  3. Click your username from the login screen (or the one your instructor provided).
  4. Enter your password and click the arrow button to reach the Desktop.

The Windows Desktop

Once logged in, you land on the Desktop — your primary work area. Key parts: the Start button (opens the Start menu), icons (shortcuts to apps and files), program windows, the taskbar with its notification area (clock, volume, network status, alerts), and the Show Desktop button in the far corner, which minimizes everything at once.

Behind the Screen: basic computer components

The processor (CPU) is the "brain" of the computer — it does all the processing, and its gigahertz (GHz) rating determines how many billions of operations it can do per second. The hard drive is permanent storage, like a filing cabinet for your files and programs; newer solid-state drives (SSDs) have no moving parts and load data much faster than traditional spinning drives. RAM is temporary working memory — much faster than the hard drive, but everything in it is lost the moment the computer loses power. A USB port is the small rectangular connector used to plug in flash drives, printers, and other equipment with a standardized cord.

Using a mouse (Hands-On 1.2)

Five basic mouse actions: Point (hold the pointer steady over something), Click (push the left button once), Double-click (click twice quickly to open a file or start a program), Drag (click, hold, and move to a new location), and Right-click (click the right button to display a pop-up menu).

  1. Point at the Recycle Bin icon on the Desktop, then point away from it.
  2. Click the Recycle Bin (don't drag) and notice it becomes selected/highlighted, then click away to deselect it.
  3. Drag the Recycle Bin to a new spot on the Desktop, then drag it back to its original location.

Passwords and account settings

Click your user icon/name at the bottom of the Start menu to open the account menu: Change account settings, Lock, and Sign out. From Account Settings you can also review Sign-In Options, connect to a Work or School network, or — with administrator privileges — add Other Users to the computer.

Signing out, switching users, and locking (Hands-On 1.3)

Signing out closes your programs and removes your login information from memory, but leaves the computer running for the next person. Switching users keeps your session saved in RAM in the background while someone else logs in — handy when a computer is shared. Locking is different again: it hides and password-protects your open work without closing anything.

  1. Click the Start button, then click your user icon/name, then choose Lock.
  2. Type your password and press Enter to unlock and return to the Desktop.

The Start menu (Hands-On 1.4-1.8)

The Start menu is where most installed apps live. A command is a link that launches or opens a file, folder, or app — like a light switch for that object. The menu has two panes: Pinned (apps you've chosen to keep handy) on top, and Recommended (recently used documents and apps) below.

  • 1.4 — Display and dismiss the Start menu: click the Start button (or press the Windows key) to open it; click it again (or press Windows again) to close it.
  • 1.5 — Launch a program: Start > All Apps > Calculator to open it, then close it with the X in the upper-right corner.
  • 1.6 — Pin and reorder an app: right-click an app in All Apps and choose Pin to Start; right-click it again in the Pinned section and choose Move to Front.
  • 1.7 — Add a folder: drag one Pinned icon onto another to create a folder, click the folder, then type a custom name (e.g. "School").
  • 1.8 — Delete a folder: drag the last icon out of a folder — once empty, the folder deletes itself automatically.

Shutting down correctly (Hands-On 1.9)

There are three ways to end your session: Sleep (low-power mode — the computer slows down, the monitor turns off, and your work stays open; wake it with the mouse or Spacebar), Shut Down (closes all programs, logs you out, and powers off — always do this at the end of the day), and Restart (shuts down and immediately powers back on, often required after installing new software).

  1. Make sure all programs are closed, then click Start > Power.
  2. Choose Sleep to pause, or Shut Down to fully power off (allow 15+ seconds).

Never hold down the physical Power button to turn off your computer — Windows needs time to close everything properly, and forcing it off can corrupt Windows or leave the computer unable to restart.

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 1.1-1.9 (above) — done together in class with instructor guidance
  • Skill Builder 1.1: Organize the Start Menu — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builder 1.1: Pin an App to the Start Menu — graded homework, see the assignment in this module
  • Chapter 1 Quiz — see the quiz in this module
  • Try This at Home (optional, on your own computer): 1.1 Switch Users, 1.2 Change Your Password, 1.3 Shut Down

items.title: Skill Builder 1.1: Organize the Start Menu
items.description:
Skill Builder 1.1: Organize the Start Menu

In this exercise, you will add app icons to the Start menu and organize the menu.

Instructions

  1. Click the Start button and click All Apps.
  2. Right-click the Clock app and choose Pin to Start.
  3. Right-click the Windows Media Player Legacy app and choose Pin to Start.
  4. Right-click the Clock app on the Pinned list and choose Move to Front. Do the same with the Windows Media Player Legacy app.
  5. Move the Clock icon from the top Pinned row to the start of the second row.
  6. Right-click the Windows Media Player Legacy app and choose Unpin from Start.
  7. Right-click the Clock app and choose Unpin from Start.

What to submit

A screenshot after step 5, showing the Clock and Windows Media Player Legacy icons pinned and reordered (before you unpin them in steps 6-7).

In this exercise, you will pin an app to the Start menu.

Instructions

  1. Click the Start button and then click All Apps.

  3. Right-click Snipping Tool and choose Pin to Start.
  4. Notice the new Snipping Tool icon at the end of the Pinned menu.

A screenshot of your Start menu showing the Snipping Tool icon pinned in the Pinned section.

items.title: Chapter 2 Overview: Starting and Controlling Apps
items.body:
Starting and Controlling Apps

This chapter is about getting comfortable running several apps at once and controlling their windows. Multitasking is the big theme: switching smoothly between apps and knowing exactly what's on screen at any moment.

Learning objectives

  • Minimize, maximize, resize, and move app windows
  • Use touch controls
  • Describe the basic features of the Windows 11 taskbar
  • Multitask effectively using the taskbar
  • Access commands using the notification area
  • Use the Action Center

Controlling app windows (Hands-On 2.1-2.2)

Every app window has quick-sizing buttons: Minimize (shrinks to just a taskbar button), Maximize (fills the screen), Restore Down (returns to its previous size), and Close. Learn one app's window controls and you can use them all. You can also drag a title bar to move a window, drag an edge or corner to resize it, and use the Snap feature to dock two windows side by side.

Touch controls (Hands-On 2.3)

If your device has a touchscreen, gestures like tap, swipe, and pinch can substitute for mouse actions. This exercise checks whether your computer supports touch.

Working with the taskbar (Hands-On 2.4-2.6)

The taskbar's notification area has four jobs: showing the system clock, showing icons for background tasks, delivering notifications, and giving quick access to specific apps. You can pin frequently used apps directly to the taskbar (2.5) and control which apps are allowed to notify you via the Action Center (2.6).

Multitasking (Hands-On 2.7-2.10)

Only one app can be active at a time, but many can be open. Practice switching between running apps (2.8), using the Flip command to cycle through them (2.9), and using Task View to see everything open at once (2.10).

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 2.1-2.10 — done together in class
  • Skill Builders 2.1-2.3 (in-book) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builders 2.1-2.2 — graded homework, see the assignments in this module
  • Chapter 2 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

items.title: Additional Skill Builder 2.1: Using the Snap Feature with Multiple Apps Open
items.description:
Additional Skill Builder 2.1: Using the Snap Feature with Multiple Apps Open

In this exercise, you will use the Snap feature to display two programs side by side on the screen.

Instructions

  1. Start the Calculator, Notepad, and Paint apps.
  2. Drag the Paint app so it snaps to the left side of the screen.
  3. Notice that Windows displays the other two apps in miniature next to Paint.
  4. Click on Notepad. Notice that it snaps to fill the right side of the screen.
  5. Close all apps.

What to submit

A screenshot showing Paint and Notepad snapped side by side.

items.title: Additional Skill Builder 2.2: Using the Show Desktop Button
items.description:
Additional Skill Builder 2.2: Using the Show Desktop Button

In this exercise, you will use the Show Desktop button to quickly minimize all open programs to see the Desktop.

Instructions

  1. Open the Notepad, Calculator, and Paint apps.
  2. Carefully click the Show Desktop button on the far-right edge of the taskbar.
  3. Notice how all the app windows are minimized.
  4. Click the Show Desktop button again. Notice that the app windows are restored onto the Desktop.
  5. Close all open apps.

What to submit

A short written response describing what happened each time you clicked the Show Desktop button.

items.title: Chapter 3 Overview: Creating an Online Account
items.body:
Creating an Online Account

This chapter introduces the Internet's online storage and access capabilities and gets you started with the Microsoft 365 online apps. You'll create a Microsoft account and connect it to your Windows 11 login so everything works together.

Learning objectives

  • Describe why we use online resources
  • Understand the basics of cloud computing
  • Create a free Microsoft account
  • Connect your Microsoft account to Windows
  • Understand account verification

Why online? (background)

The cloud refers to storing apps and services on the Internet rather than only on your own computer. Microsoft 365 for the web is a free, browser-based version of Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and more) — different from the full desktop versions, but sharing the same core features.

Creating your Microsoft account (Hands-On 3.1-3.2)

You'll create a Microsoft account (3.1) that gets used throughout the rest of this course, then connect that account to your Windows 11 login (3.2) so you're automatically signed in to Microsoft services.

Logging in to OneDrive and Microsoft 365 for the web (Hands-On 3.3-3.4)

Once connected, you can log in to OneDrive directly through Microsoft Edge (3.3) and launch apps like Word Online from there (3.4), using the app launcher to jump between Microsoft's online apps.

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 3.1-3.4 — done together in class
  • This chapter has no Skill Builder exercises (in-book or Additional) — it's shorter, focused purely on account setup
  • Chapter 3 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

items.title: Chapter 4 Overview: Working with Apps
items.body:
Working with Apps

This chapter uses the Paint and Word Online apps as learning platforms for skills you'll use constantly: typing, editing, formatting, cutting, copying, pasting, and saving files. You'll also get comfortable with menus, toolbars, and Ribbons, and how the mouse pointer changes depending on what it's doing.

Learning objectives

  • Use common features found in drop-down menus, toolbars and Ribbons, and scroll bars
  • Use the mouse effectively as the appearance and function of the mouse pointer changes
  • Type and edit text in an app
  • Cut or copy text and then paste it into another location
  • Save files or copies of files on OneDrive

App commands (Hands-On 4.1)

Modern Office apps use a Ribbon — a toolbar organized by task, with tabs like Home, Insert, and Layout. Older apps often use classic drop-down menus instead. Either way, the mouse pointer changes shape depending on the tool selected.

Saving your work (Hands-On 4.2-4.4)

Nothing is permanently saved until you tell the computer to save it — until then it's just sitting in RAM, temporary memory. You'll draw something in Paint (4.2), then save it to three different locations: your hard drive, a USB flash drive, and OneDrive (4.3). Filenames can't use the characters | \ ? * < " : > /. Mouse pointers change shape in Paint depending on the tool (4.4).

The work area (Hands-On 4.5)

When content is too big to fit in the window, scroll bars let you navigate around it.

Typing and editing in Word Online (Hands-On 4.6-4.10)

You'll type a message (4.6), select text (4.7) — text must be selected before it can be edited or formatted — format it with bold, italics, and font changes (4.8), print it (4.9), and save it as a PDF (4.10).

Cut, copy, and paste (Hands-On 4.11)

Cut and Copy both place a copy of the item on the Clipboard; Cut also removes the original. Keyboard shortcuts: Ctrl+X (Cut), Ctrl+C (Copy), Ctrl+V (Paste).

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 4.1-4.11 — done together in class
  • Skill Builders 4.1-4.2 (in-book: Create and Save a Letter from Start to Finish; Create a Copy of Your Letter) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builders 4.1-4.2 (Information Letter; Copy and Paste) — graded homework, see the assignments in this module
  • Chapter 4 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

items.title: Additional Skill Builder 4.1: Information Letter
items.description:
Additional Skill Builder 4.1: Information Letter

In this exercise, you will write and edit a basic letter asking for more information about educational opportunities.

Instructions

  1. Open Word Online and create a new Blank Document.
  2. Type the letter:
    TO: Smithsonian Institute
    FROM: [Enter Your Name Here]
    RE: Educational Opportunities

    To Whom It May Concern;

    I will be travelling to Washington DC in the coming months and will have a few days to explore the Smithsonian Institute.

    Since I only have a few days, I was hoping you could send me information on what exhibits and educational opportunities a US History buff should partake in while at the Smithsonian.

    Your help would be greatly appreciated.

    Sincerely,

    [Enter Your Name Here]
  3. Select "US History buff" and replace with: United States history enthusiast
  4. Select all of the text and change the Font to Arial and the Font Size to 12.
  5. Rename the document: Information Letter
  6. Close Word Online.

What to submit

The finished "Information Letter" document.

items.title: Additional Skill Builder 4.2: Copy and Paste
items.description:
Additional Skill Builder 4.2: Copy and Paste

In this exercise, you will copy text from your Information Letter into a new letter. Complete Additional Skill Builder 4.1 first.

Instructions

  1. Start Word Online and create a new Blank Document.
  2. In the new document, type:
    TO: Library of Congress
    FROM: [Insert Your Name Here]
    RE: Educational Opportunities
  3. Open your "Information Letter" document from OneDrive.
  4. Select the text from "To Whom It May Concern" through the end of the letter, including your name.
  5. Press Ctrl+C to copy the text.
  6. Switch to your new document and position the insertion point on the blank line below "RE: Educational Opportunities."
  7. Press Ctrl+V to paste the text.
  8. Replace "Smithsonian Institute" (2nd paragraph) and "Smithsonian" (3rd paragraph) with: Library of Congress
  9. Select all the text (Ctrl+A) and change the Font to Arial, Font Size 12.
  10. Rename the document: Information Letter 2
  11. Close both documents.

What to submit

The finished "Information Letter 2" document.

items.title: Chapter 5 Overview: Using Email
items.body:
Using Email

This chapter covers the Outlook Online app and the fundamentals of email: the parts of an inbox and a message, sending/receiving/replying, attaching files, organizing with folders, and protecting yourself from malicious email.

Learning objectives

  • Create a properly formatted email address
  • Send and receive emails, including those with attachments
  • Create folders and organize emails using Outlook
  • Identify spam and other email threats

What is email? The Outlook Online app (Hands-On 5.1-5.2)

You'll log in to Outlook via OneDrive (5.1) and read a message from the Outlook Team (5.2), getting familiar with the Outlook screen and its dynamic, responsive layout.

Sending, receiving, and replying (Hands-On 5.3-5.5)

Send a message (5.3), send one with an attachment (5.4), and reply to a message from your instructor (5.5). Every message needs an address line and message body — the subject line is technically optional but recommended.

Saving emails with folders (Hands-On 5.6-5.7)

Create folders to organize your Inbox (5.6), then move messages into them using both drag-and-drop and the Move To command (5.7).

Email safety (Hands-On 5.8)

Learn to spot and remove spam using the Report Junk command. Deleted emails move to the Deleted folder and are permanently removed after about ten days.

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 5.1-5.8 — done together in class
  • Skill Builders 5.1-5.5 (in-book: Save Files from Links; Create a Gmail Account; Send/Read Email in Gmail; Delete/Archive in Gmail; Forward an Email) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builders 5.1-5.2 (Multiple Address Lines; Organize Email with Folders) — graded homework, see the assignments in this module
  • Chapter 5 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

items.title: Additional Skill Builder 5.2: Organize Your Email with Folders
items.description:
Additional Skill Builder 5.2: Organize Your Email with Folders

In this exercise, you will create a folder in Outlook.com to organize your email messages. If you don't have any emails yet, send yourself three messages first.

Instructions

  1. Start Outlook.com.
  2. Click Create New Folder on the Folders menu, type "Messages to keep," and press Enter.
  3. Drag the "Messages to keep" folder on top of the Inbox folder so it becomes a subfolder of the Inbox.
  4. Click the Inbox folder.
  5. Choose an email message and drag it onto the "Messages to keep" folder.
  6. Click the "Messages to keep" folder and verify the email is there.
  7. Close Outlook.com.

items.title: Chapter 6 Overview: Finding Files
items.body:
Finding Files

This chapter starts Unit 2: File Management. You'll navigate drives and folders, learn to safely use a flash drive, get comfortable with File Explorer, and learn to find files with Search.

Learning objectives

  • Describe and use various storage devices
  • Use File Explorer to locate files and folders
  • Plug in a USB flash drive
  • Identify different types of folders used by Windows
  • Find files and folders with File Search

About storage media (Hands-On 6.1-6.2)

View the storage drives on your computer (6.1) — each is assigned a letter (usually C: for the main internal hard drive). Then practice plugging in, viewing, and safely removing a USB flash drive (6.2) — never unplug while the activity light is on.

File Explorer (Hands-On 6.3-6.7)

File Explorer lets you view your computer's drives and their contents. Practice navigating with the address bar (6.3), the Back/Forward buttons (6.4), sorting folders (6.5), the Folders pane for a full-tree view (6.6), and opening multiple tabs at once (6.7).

Searching for files (Hands-On 6.8)

Use Windows Search to find files across This PC — a huge time-saver once you have a lot of files, even if they're well organized.

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 6.1-6.8 — done together in class
  • Skill Builders 6.1-6.2 (in-book: Find the Remaining Capacity of a Drive; Search the Contents of Files) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builders 6.1-6.2 (Changing the View of the Folder Pane; Safely Removing a USB Flash Drive) — graded homework, see the assignments in this module
  • Chapter 6 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

items.title: Chapter 7 Overview: Storing Files
items.body:
Storing Files

This chapter is about organizing your digital life: creating folders and subfolders, moving/copying files, deleting and restoring them, and using OneDrive to store files in the cloud.

Learning objectives

  • Create new folders and subfolders for organizing your files
  • Move or copy folders and files from one location to another
  • Delete folders and files and, if necessary, restore them from the Recycle Bin
  • Use OneDrive to store your files and folders
  • Upload to and download from OneDrive

Creating folders (Hands-On 7.1-7.2)

Create a new folder on the Desktop (7.1) and on your flash drive (7.2). Folders can be nested inside other folders (subfolders) as many times as needed. Folder names can be up to 255 characters.

Moving and copying (Hands-On 7.3-7.5)

Practice the Cut/Copy/Paste method (7.3), drag-and-drop (7.4) — new users often find the right-click drag-and-drop easier, since it gives more control over what happens when you drop the file — and selecting multiple files at once (7.5).

Deleting and restoring (Hands-On 7.6)

Items deleted from an internal or external hard drive go to the Recycle Bin and can be restored; items deleted from a USB flash drive do NOT go to the Recycle Bin — they're gone.

OneDrive file storage (Hands-On 7.7-7.10)

Create a folder in OneDrive (7.7), navigate between folders (7.8), upload files to OneDrive (7.9), and download from OneDrive back to your computer (7.10).

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 7.1-7.10 — done together in class
  • Skill Builders 7.1-7.3 (in-book: Find and Copy Files; Open a File Directly from OneDrive; Create a File and Upload to OneDrive) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builders 7.1-7.2 (Downloading a File from OneDrive; Dragging a Folder to Your USB Flash Drive) — graded homework, see the assignments in this module
  • Chapter 7 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

In this exercise, you will create a file on your OneDrive storage, download it to your computer, and then move it to your USB flash drive.

  1. Start OneDrive and plug in your USB flash drive.

items.title: Chapter 8 Overview: Using the Internet

Using the Internet

This chapter starts Unit 3: The Internet and More. You'll learn the origins of the Internet and the web, how to connect, and how to use Microsoft Edge to browse effectively.

The Internet and browsing (Hands-On 8.1-8.3)

The World Wide Web isn't the same thing as the Internet — it's one piece of technology that runs on it. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a website's unique address. Navigate to a web page (8.1), use tabbed browsing to have multiple pages open at once (8.2), and print a web page (8.3, cancelled before actually printing).

Favorites (Hands-On 8.4-8.7)

Create a Favorite (8.4), turn on the Favorites Bar (8.5), organize Favorites into folders (8.6), and remove one you no longer need (8.7). A busy, disorganized Favorites list defeats its own purpose.

items.title: Chapter 9 Overview: Researching on the Internet
items.body:
Researching on the Internet

This chapter covers how search engines work and how to search effectively, then moves into protecting yourself from web threats.

Learning objectives

  • Use Google to perform a basic search
  • Use Google to search for images
  • Protect yourself from web threats
  • Complete a complicated search

Performing a basic web search (Hands-On 9.1-9.2)

Search engines index the web and match items to your keywords — they don't search the entire web instantly on demand. Being more specific in your search terms gets more relevant results. Practice a basic Google search (9.1) and a Google image search (9.2). Be aware of copyright when using images found online.

Defending yourself from web threats

A firewall checks data entering your computer and blocks anything that looks like a threat — Windows comes with one built in. Antivirus software needs to be updated regularly, since new viruses appear daily. On social media, remember that anything you post can stay on the Internet forever.

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 9.1-9.2 — done together in class
  • Skill Builders 9.1-9.4 (in-book: Search for Copyright-Safe Images; Save an Image; Clear Browsing Data; Search for News) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builder 9.1 (Searching for Images with Bing) — graded homework, see the assignment in this module
  • Chapter 9 Quiz — see the quiz in this module

items.title: Chapter 10 Overview: Using Settings and Help
items.body:
Using Settings and Help

The final chapter: Windows Search, Settings (screen, power, updates), and the Store. Several exercises here use WebSims — since they involve system-level settings — via the Labyrinth Student Resource Center rather than direct hands-on practice in a shared lab computer.

Learning objectives

  • Search your computer using the new Search program
  • Change the screen resolution and Desktop background
  • Change the power options
  • Update Windows 11

Searching Windows and the web (Hands-On 10.1-10.3)

The Search box on the taskbar searches both your computer and the web at once. Practice a basic search (10.1), searching the web from Windows Search (10.2), and getting help for a specific app like File Explorer (10.3).

Using Settings (Hands-On 10.4-10.7, WebSims)

Settings has nine basic categories and covers most day-to-day configuration; the Control Panel still exists for legacy options. These four exercises use WebSims (browser-based simulations) since they touch system date/time, power, and update settings that shouldn't be changed on a shared lab computer: checking automatic date/time (10.4), power and battery options (10.5), the power plan (10.6), and Windows Update options (10.7).

Controlling the screen and the Store (Hands-On 10.8-10.9)

Higher screen resolution means more, smaller pixels. Browse the Microsoft Store's app categories (10.8) and use a WebSim to download the free Netflix app (10.9).

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 10.1-10.9 — done together in class (10.4-10.7 and 10.9 via WebSim)
  • Skill Builder 10.1 (in-book: Change the Screen Resolution, WebSim) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
